intro.why: Training large models is limited more by memory and memory traffic than by raw arithmetic. These techniques are why billion-parameter models and 100k-token contexts are trainable at all, and they reappear in serving (M5–M6).

symbols: sequence length, batch, hidden size, layers
running max and running sum in online softmax

sections.title: Where training memory goes
sections.plain: GPU memory fills with weights, their gradients, optimizer bookkeeping, and saved intermediate values.
sections.body:
Training a big model is limited less by speed and more by memory. Four things fill the GPU:

  • Weights: the parameters.
  • Gradients: one per weight.
  • Optimizer states: extra numbers per weight (Adam keeps two).
  • Activations: intermediate values saved during the forward pass for the backward pass; they grow with batch size, sequence length, width and depth.

A rough activation estimate is ≈ 34·s·b·h·L bytes in 16-bit (excluding attention scores): for sequence 2048, batch 8, hidden 4096 and 32 layers, about 73 GB, often more than the weights' bill. Activation checkpointing stores only each layer's input and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading roughly one extra forward pass for most of that memory.

sections.title: The memory bill of Adam
sections.plain: With Adam in 32-bit, each parameter costs about 16 bytes before activations.
sections.body:
Adam keeps a momentum and a variance estimate per weight, usually in 32-bit. Per parameter: weights 4 bytes + gradients 4 bytes + Adam states 8 bytes:

$$4 + 4 + 8 = 16\ \text{bytes per parameter}$$

Worked: a 1-billion-parameter model needs about 16 GB just for weights, gradients and optimizer states, before any activations; a 70B model about 1.1 TB, far beyond one 80 GB GPU. The optimizer states are the biggest single cost. Plain SGD needs no state; momentum SGD needs 4 bytes.

This is why large-scale training shards these tensors across GPUs (ZeRO / fully sharded data parallel): each device keeps only its slice of the states, gradients and, optionally, weights.

sections.title: Mixed-precision training
sections.plain: Do most maths and storage in 16-bit, keep a 32-bit master copy of the weights, and scale the loss so tiny gradients survive.
sections.body:
Mixed precision stores activations and runs matrix multiplications in 16-bit (fp16 or bf16), roughly halving activation memory and making maths much faster on tensor cores. Three ingredients:

  1. 16-bit compute for forward and backward passes.
  2. An fp32 master copy of the weights, updated with fp32 optimizer states, so small updates aren't rounded away.
  3. Loss scaling (for fp16): multiply the loss by S (e.g. 2¹⁰) before backpropagation so small gradients don't underflow, then divide by S before the update. A gradient of 10⁻⁸ becomes 0 in fp16 but survives when scaled.

fp16 has a narrow range (≈6×10⁻⁸ to 65,504); bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range with less precision, so it rarely needs loss scaling and is now common. Note that with the fp32 master copy and Adam, weights + gradients + states remain about 2 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes/param; the halving comes from activations and speed. Everyday picture: weighing ingredients to the gram rather than the milligram: accurate enough and much faster.

sections.title: Attention's quadratic cost
sections.plain: Every token compares itself with every other token, so doubling the length quadruples the work.
sections.body:
Self-attention computes an n × n score matrix per head per layer:

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V,\qquad \text{cost} \propto n^2 d$$

n = 2000 costs 4× n = 1000. At n = 128,000 a single head's score matrix would hold 1.6 × 10¹⁰ entries, about 33 GB in fp16, for every head in every layer. Long inputs are therefore expensive in both compute and memory, and the memory traffic of writing and re-reading that matrix is often the real bottleneck.

sections.title: IO-aware FlashAttention
sections.plain: Compute attention in small tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory and never store the whole score matrix.
sections.body:
GPUs have a little very fast on-chip memory (SRAM) and a lot of slower main memory (HBM). Standard attention writes the full n × n matrix to HBM and reads it back several times. FlashAttention is IO-aware: it loads blocks of Q, K and V into SRAM, computes scores for one tile, and accumulates the output using an online softmax (running max m and running sum ℓ, rescaling earlier partial results when a larger score appears).

Worked: one query row with scores [2, 1, 3, 0] in two blocks. Block 1: m = 2, ℓ = e⁰ + e⁻¹ = 1.368. Block 2: new max 3, rescale ℓ by e⁻¹: 1.368 × 0.368 + e⁰ + e⁻³ = 1.553, exactly the full softmax denominator (0.368 + 0.135 + 1 + 0.050). The result is exact, not approximate; code example ex2 matches standard attention to ~10⁻¹⁶.

Same answer, far fewer memory trips, memory linear in n: faster training and longer contexts. (Picture working on one block of a spreadsheet at your desk instead of carrying the whole thing back and forth to the filing cabinet.)

sections.title: Ring Attention and long context
sections.plain: Spread a very long sequence across several devices that pass key/value blocks around in a ring.
sections.body:
Even with FlashAttention, one device can only hold so many tokens' keys, values and activations. Ring Attention splits the sequence across P devices. Each keeps its block of queries; key/value blocks are passed around a ring. In each of P rounds a device computes (tiled) attention between its queries and the block it currently holds, then forwards the block, overlapping communication with computation. After P − 1 passes every query has met every key.

Context length then scales with the number of devices (e.g. 1,000,000 tokens on 8 devices = 125,000 queries each). Total work remains O(n²); it is distributed, not removed. Long-context training also typically needs RoPE rescaling (M3) and curricula of progressively longer sequences.

sections.title: Sparse and linear attention variants
sections.plain: Let each token look at only some tokens, or approximate attention so cost grows linearly.
sections.body:
To reduce the work itself, attention variants trade some accuracy for scale:

  • Sparse attention: attend to a subset (local blocks, strided positions, a few global tokens).
  • Sliding-window attention: each token sees only the previous w tokens (cost ∝ n·w); stacked layers still pass information further.
  • Linear / sub-quadratic attention: kernel feature maps or state-space-style recurrences make cost ∝ n·d.

At n = 128k: full ≈ 1.6×10¹⁰ score operations, window 4096 ≈ 5.2×10⁸, linear (d = 64) ≈ 8×10⁶. The catch: approximate variants can lose quality, especially precise recall of distant details. Use them when context length truly demands it; many models mix full-attention and windowed layers. Lower precision can also cause numerical trouble if done carelessly, hence master weights and loss scaling.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Parallelism types: data, tensor, pipeline and sequence/context parallelism combine to train the largest models.
  • 8-bit optimizers and fp8 training push memory and speed further with careful scaling.
  • FlashAttention is exact: it changes the order of computation, not the result (up to floating-point rounding).
  • Memory, not FLOPs: many kernels are bandwidth-bound; counting bytes moved is as important as counting operations.

code.title: Memory bill, mixed precision and loss scaling
code.explain: Totals bytes per parameter for fp32 + Adam (4 + 4 + 8 = 16 → 16 GB per billion parameters) and mixed precision (2 + 2 + 4 + 8), estimates activation memory for several sequence/batch sizes, and shows a 10⁻⁸ gradient underflowing to 0 in fp16, recovered by loss scaling, while bf16 keeps it.
mistakes: Claiming mixed precision halves optimizer memory.
Forgetting to unscale gradients before the update.
code.notes: Activation formula is a rough rule of thumb.
code.code:
"""Training memory per parameter, mixed precision, and why loss scaling is needed in fp16."""
import numpy as np

def gb(bytes_): return bytes_ / 1e9
N = 1e9
fp32 = {"weights": 4, "gradients": 4, "Adam m + v": 8}
mixed = {"fp16/bf16 weights": 2, "fp16/bf16 gradients": 2, "fp32 master weights": 4, "Adam m + v (fp32)": 8}
for name, d in (("full fp32 + Adam", fp32), ("mixed precision + Adam", mixed)):
    tot = sum(d.values())
    print(f"{name:24s}: " + " + ".join(f"{v}" for v in d.values()) + f" = {tot} bytes/param -> {gb(tot*N):.0f} GB for 1B params")
print("note: mixed precision mainly halves ACTIVATION memory and speeds up matmuls; the weight+optimizer")
print("      bill stays ~16 B/param because of the fp32 master copy (sharding, e.g. ZeRO, is what cuts it).")

# Activation memory grows with batch and sequence length (rough per-layer estimate ~ 34*s*b*h bytes in 16-bit)
h, L = 4096, 32
for s, b in ((2048, 1), (2048, 8), (8192, 8)):
    act = 34 * s * b * h * L
    print(f"activations (rough) seq {s:5d}, batch {b}: {gb(act):6.1f} GB in 16-bit; {gb(2*act):6.1f} GB if kept in fp32")

# fp16 range: tiny gradients underflow to zero; scaling the loss rescues them
g = np.array([1e-8, 1e-6, 2e-4], dtype=np.float32)
print("gradients in fp32:          ", g)
print("cast to fp16:               ", g.astype(np.float16), " <- 1e-8 underflows to 0")
S = 1024
gs = (g * S).astype(np.float16)
print(f"scaled by {S}, fp16:         ", gs)
print("unscaled in fp32 afterwards:", gs.astype(np.float32) / S)
print("bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range (8 bits) with less precision, so it rarely needs loss scaling:")
for x in (1e-8, 1e-6, 65504 * 2):
    b = np.frombuffer(np.array([x], np.float32).tobytes(), np.uint32)[0] & 0xFFFF0000
    with np.errstate(over="ignore"): print(f"   {x:9.2e} -> bf16 {np.frombuffer(np.uint32(b).tobytes(), np.float32)[0]:9.3e}   fp16 {np.float16(x):9.3e}")

code.title: Quadratic cost, tiled attention and ring attention
code.explain: Tabulates n² score memory up to 128k tokens (~33 GB per head per layer), implements tiled attention with an online softmax and checks it equals standard attention (max difference ~5×10⁻¹⁶), compares memory traffic, and sketches ring attention and the cost of window/linear variants.
mistakes: Forgetting to rescale the running output when the max changes.
Thinking ring attention reduces total work.
code.notes: Real FlashAttention runs as a fused GPU kernel.
code.code:
"""Attention cost vs length, tiled attention with an online softmax (the FlashAttention idea),
and how ring attention splits a long sequence across devices."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

for n in (1000, 2000, 8000, 128000):
    print(f"n = {n:6d}: score matrix n^2 = {n*n:.2e} entries; fp16 = {2*n*n/1e9:7.2f} GB per head per layer")

n, d, B = 512, 64, 64
Q, K, V = (rng.normal(size=(n, d)) for _ in range(3))
S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True)); P /= P.sum(1, keepdims=True)
O_std = P @ V

# Tiled: process key/value blocks one at a time, keeping running max m, running sum l and output acc
O = np.zeros((n, d)); m = np.full(n, -np.inf); l = np.zeros(n)
for j in range(0, n, B):
    Sj = Q @ K[j:j+B].T / np.sqrt(d)
    m_new = np.maximum(m, Sj.max(1))
    scale = np.exp(m - m_new)
    Pj = np.exp(Sj - m_new[:, None])
    l = l * scale + Pj.sum(1)
    O = O * scale[:, None] + Pj @ V[j:j+B]
    m = m_new
O /= l[:, None]
print(f"max |tiled - standard| = {np.abs(O - O_std).max():.2e}  (same answer, exact up to rounding)")
print(f"largest temporary: standard {n*n} scores vs tiled {n*B} scores per block ({n*n//(n*B)}x smaller)")

# Rough HBM traffic: standard writes and re-reads the n x n matrix; tiled keeps it on-chip
std_io = 2 * (3 * n * d) + 4 * n * n
tiled_io = 2 * (3 * n * d) + 2 * n * d * (n // B)
print(f"approx memory reads/writes (elements): standard {std_io:,} vs tiled {tiled_io:,}")

# Ring attention: P devices each hold n/P query rows and pass K/V blocks around the ring
Pdev, n_long = 8, 1_000_000
print(f"ring attention: {n_long:,} tokens on {Pdev} devices -> {n_long//Pdev:,} queries each; "
      f"K/V blocks rotate {Pdev - 1} times; each device never holds more than 2 blocks of K/V")
for name, cost in (("full", lambda n: n*n), ("sliding window w=4096", lambda n: n*4096), ("linear", lambda n: n*64)):
    print(f"  {name:22s}: score ops at n = 128k -> {cost(128000):.2e}")
